Pediatric diarrhea = excessive daily stool; liquid volume > 10 mL stool/kg body weight/day

Functional/idiopathic constipation, slow transit

Secondary (r/o)

Metabolic: hypothyroidism, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia, diabetes

Structural: colorectal cancer, benign strictures, pseudo-obstruction

Neurologic/myopathies: Parkinson’s disease, MS, spinal cord injury, autonomic neuropathy, Hirschsprung’s, immobility, botulism,

hollow visceral myopathy, cerebral palsy, muscular dystrophy

Medications: opiates, anticholinergics, calcium (antacids), iron supplements, antiparkinsonian drugs (dopamine), lead toxicity

Systemic: trisomy 21, cystic fibrosis, connective tissue disorders, celiac disease, cow’s milk allergy

Defecatory disorders

Anismus: the paradoxical contraction of the anal sphincter rather than relaxing during attempted defecation

(involve GI/general surgery)

Dyssynergia: any disturbance of muscular coordination, resulting in uncoordinated and abrupt movements

Rectocele: a bulging of the front wall of the rectum into the back wall of the vagina

Constipation workup
  • Hx: symptoms of constipation, dietary Hx (fibre/water intake), adequate time for toileting, willingness to use public bathrooms,
  • PMHx (look for 2° causes), medications, allergies, social Hx (ADLs, IADLs, abuse)
  • PEx: DRE, inspect for anal fissures/hemorrhoids/soiling, assess anal tone at rest and with squeeze, palpate for rectal mass,

exclude fecal impaction

  • Ix: CBC, calcium, TSH, colonoscopy (indicated for red flags)

Choosing Wisely: avoid performing a colonoscopy for constipation in those under the age of 50 years without family

o

history of colon cancer or alarm features

  • Colon transit study: ingestion of 24 radio-opaque sitz markers on day 1; AXR on day 5
  • Anorectal manometry and balloon expulsion test: specialized pressure sensing catheter and inflatable balloon inserted into the

rectum to measure rectal sensation, anal pressure, anorectal inhibitory reflex, and ability to expel balloon

  • Defecating proctogram: barium instilled into rectum then defecation on a special commode under x-rays allows for the

visualization of anatomic abnormalities

  • Tx: patient education, dietary/lifestyle (adequate fluid intake, 20-30 g/day of fibre, physical activity), osmotic laxatives (17 g

PEG3350 dissolved in 8 oz water; 15-30 cc lactulose; magnesium-based), stimulant laxatives (1 tab senna, 5 mg bisacodyl), stool

softeners (100 mg docusate b.i.d., 15 mL mineral oil NOT recommended), enemas (sodium phosphate, tap water, soap suds),

secretagogues (linaclotide – 145 mcg for constipation, 290 mcg for IBS-C; prucalopride), surgery (subtotal colectomy and

ileorectal anastomosis, repair of rectocele), biofeedback (relaxation/coordination retraining of the pelvic floor)

Long-term use of laxatives will NOT lead to dependency and a “lazy colon”

GI Tip of the Day

2022-03-07

The 2 most common causes of a patient presenting with dysphagia and a documented history of weight loss are esophageal cancer and achalasia.

Other causes of dysphagia, such as peptic stricture, are much less likely to result in significant weight loss unless very severe.

2022-03-08

An EGD with esophageal biopsies needs to be considered in a patient with intermittent solid-food dysphagia to rule out eosinophilic esophagitis

(EoE) even in the presence of normal endoscopic findings. Eosinophil counts > 15 per hpf in the mid or proximal esophagus is extremely suggestive

of EoE and can be treated with PPI, swallowed topical steroids & esophageal dilation.

2022-03-09

The tip for today pertains to GI history taking. For any GI and liver-related illness, always ask about NSAIDs. It is also important to always take a

detailed social history including smoking, alcohol, marijuana, and other recreational drug use. Don’t forget to elucidate any family history of GI

related malignancy, IBD, celiac or liver disease. Finally, asking about any previous endoscopic evaluations can help to determine the need for

further endoscopic investigation.

2022-03-10

Typical symptoms of GERD (i.e. heartburn & regurgitation) are the most likely to respond to treatment with Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs). Other

symptoms potentially associated with GERD include: cough, shortness of breath, hoarseness of voice and dental enamel erosion. These so called

“extra esophageal” symptoms of GERD are less likely to respond to PPIs, mainly because they are less likely to be actually caused by GERD. If in

doubt whether the symptoms are related to GERD or not, a 24 hour pH study can be helpful.

2022-03-11

Cyclical attacks of nausea and vomiting, known as Cannabis Hyperemesis Syndrome (CHS), have been reported with the long-term use of

marijuana; It is generally associated with heavy users of THC (i.e. Daily use for months to years) and patients often report compulsive bathing in hot

water as this may relieve their symptoms. The only effective treatment is Cannabis cessation.

2022-03-21

Weight loss is not a typical symptom of IBS, so in a patient presenting with possible IBS and weight loss other causes need to be excluded. For

treatment of IBS always remember dietary interventions (i.e. low FODMAPs diet), psychosocial interventions and tailor medical therapy based on

predominant symptom complex.

2022-03-22

Always consider whether a digital rectal exam is necessary when examining a patient with GI symptoms. This simple exam is often overlooked and

can be quite useful and even lifesaving if pathology such as a rectal mass is found. This should always be performed in a patient presenting with

rectal bleeding. Ensure patients are informed about what you are going to be doing, obtain consent and drape patient appropriately. Remember to

always have a chaperone present. There are very few contraindications to rectal exam: febrile neutropenia, no anus, no finger!

2022-03-23

If suspicious for celiac disease, one can screen by ordering TTG antibodies. Always remember to order an IgA level anytime you order TTG

antibodies, because TTG can be falsely negative if IgA is low. If TTG antibodies are positive, one should always go on to confirm the diagnosis with

endoscopy and duodenal biopsies. Iron-deficiency anemia is the most common extraintestinal manifestation of celiac disease.

2022-03-24

When working up iron deficiency anemia, don’t forget to treat the iron deficiency while investigations are pending!! Do not use serum iron to

diagnose iron deficiency anemia… use ferritin or transferrin saturation instead as they are a more reliable indicator of actual iron stores.

2022-03-25

Remember melena is more typical of an Upper GI bleed but occasionally can be a manifestation of a proximal Lower GI bleed. Similarly, bright red

blood per rectum, is usually a manifestation of a lower GI bleed, but one always needs to be alert to the possibility that it represents a brisk Upper

GI bleed, which would be suggested if the patient is hemodynamically unstable. The most important management principal for GI bleeds is to

always resuscitate the patient aggressively first, then consider scoping them!

2022-03-28

All patients with chronic liver disease, with or without cirrhosis, should be vaccinated for Hep A and Hep B, unless they have active infection or are

serologically immune. If a patient with compensated liver disease were to acquire an active infection with either Hepatitis A or Hepatitis B, this can

lead to severe decompensation and this can be prevented through vaccination.

2022-03-29

Early liver cirrhosis can be present with a normal appearing liver on imaging in addition to normal liver enzymes and synthetic liver bloodwork.

High clinical suspicion is necessary. Unexplained splenomegaly, dilated portal vein, and thrombocytopenia can be early clues to the presence of

cirrhosis.

2022-03-30

Statins are safe to use in patients with cirrhosis. Liver enzymes should be routinely monitored, and these medications can be continued as long as

liver enzymes do not elevate more than 2 times from baseline after starting statins.

2022-03-31

Typically they should be progressed from clear fluids to full fluids to diet as tolerated. If symptoms recur with reintroduction of food, then you may

have to back off temporarily and if prolonged NPO is expected or required may need to consider supplemental nutrition with NJ tube or rarely TPN.

2022-04-01

In patients with hepatic encephalopathy ammonia does not correlate with the degree of encephalopathy and should not be used in the diagnosis,

rather the clinical assessment is key in making the diagnosis.

Acute liver failure: coagulopathy (INR ≥ 1.5), neurologic dysfunction with any degree of hepatic encephalopathy, no prior evidence

of liver disease, disease course of ≤ 26 weeks

  • Acetaminophen, drug-induced liver injury, HBV, HAV, autoimmunity, ischemia, Wilson’s disease, Budd-Chiari, pregnancy
  • Ix: serum chemistries, hepatic panel, arterial blood, toxicologic, hematologic, viral hepatitis serologies, autoimmune markers,

urine, serum ceruloplasmin, blood cultures, ECG, imaging

  • Tx: routine monitoring, glucose infusions, stress ulcer prophylaxis, restrict clotting factors unless active bleeding, N-

acetylcysteine, avoid sedatives and hepatotoxic/nephrotoxic drugs

  • Hepatic encephalopathy: transfer to critical care at first symptoms of mental alterations; quiet surrounding, elevate head of

bed, intubate, ventilate, sedate; empirical ABX; normalize biochemical variables (Na, Mg, PO4, K)

King’s College Criteria for acute liver failure
Paracetamol-Induced ALF

Non-Paracetamol Induced ALF

Arterial blood pH < 7.3 (irrespective of grade of encephalopathy)

Prothrombin time > 100 s (INR > 6.5) (irrespective of grade of encephalopathy)

OR all of the following:

OR any 3 of the following (irrespective of grade of encephalopathy)

  • Prothrombin time > 100 s (INR > 6.5)
  • Age < 10 or > 40 years
  • Serum creatinine > 300 𝜇mol/L
  • Etiology: non-A/B hepatitis, drug-induced
  • Grade III or IV hepatic encephalopathy
  • Duration of jaundice to encephalopathy > 7 days
  • Prothrombin time > 50 (INR > 3.5)
  • Serum bilirubin > 300 𝜇mol/L
Chronic hepatitis: > 6 months
  • Viral (HBV, HCV, HDV), autoimmune (autoimmune hepatitis, PBC, PSC, IgG4 cholangiopathy), chronic biliary disease (recurrent

bacterial cholangitis, bile duct stenosis), cardiovascular (Budd-Chiari syndrome, RHF, Osler disease), storage diseases

(hemochromatosis, Wilson’s disease, alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency), medications (methotrexate, amiodarone), porphyria, fatty

liver diseases (alcoholic liver disease, NAFLD), veno-occlusive disease, neonatal hepatitis syndromes, cryptogenic (NASH)

Autoimmune hepatitis: immune system attacks liver cells
  • Asymptomatic, fatigue, nausea, pruritis
  • Ix: high IgG, anti-nuclear Ab, anti-smooth muscle Ab, liver biopsy (portal and periportal lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate)
  • Tx: prednisone, azathioprine

Alcoholic hepatitis: reversible inflammatory liver damage caused by sustained,

long-term alcohol consumption

  • Direct toxicity from ethanol and its metabolites and oxidative damage

disrupts the function of the cell and mitochondrial membranes leading to

lipid accumulation

  • Classic presentation: symptomatic, nausea, malaise, tachycardia, fever
  • Hepatic failure/portal hypertension: ascites, coagulopathy, significant

hematemesis from ruptured esophageal varices, encephalopathy (asterixis,

altered mental status), RUQ tenderness, hepatomegaly

  • Dx: bloodwork (AST >> ALT, ↑ INR), histology (steatosis, neutrophilic

infiltrate, centrilobular balloon necrosis of hepatocytes, Mallory bodies)

  • Tx: abstinence from alcohol, IV folate and thiamine, IV glucose solution,

vitamin K, fresh frozen plasma, prednisolone

Alcohol cirrhosis: final and irreversible form of alcoholic liver disease

  • Tx: alcohol abstinence; nutritional support (frequent small quantity feeding, micronutrient/vitamin replacement, high protein

and kilocalorie), liver transplantation, psychosocial support, smoking cessation, avoid hepatotoxic agents, vaccination (HAV,

HBV, pneumococcus, influenza)

  • Metabolic syndrome (DM, hypertension, central obesity, dyslipidemia), rapid weight loss, infections, drugs/toxins
  • Histology: macrovesicular/macrovesicular steatosis → cellular ballooning → necrosis
  • Tx: lifestyle (diet, exercise), review medications, minimize EtOH, optimize management of comorbidities (statins = safe; screen

for PCOS, hypothyroidism, obstructive sleep apnea)

Cirrhosis (chronic liver damage): the irreversible scarring of the liver that occurs after years of chronic insult

  • Cell death → progressive fibrosis → regenerative nodule formation; liver is shrunken, firm, and nodular
  • Severely impaired liver function, jaundice, pruritis, hypoalbuminemia, hypoestrogenism, anemia, coagulopathies, splenomegaly,

thrombocytopenia, portal hypertension

  • Dx: biopsy (gold standard), AST and ALT may be elevated or normal (hepatocytes “burn out”), ultrasound
  • Tx: liver transplantation
Ascites: the accumulation of fluid in the abdominal cavity
  • The most common complication in patients with cirrhosis; 60% of patients develop ascites within 10 years of cirrhosis Dx
  • PEx: shifting dullness, fluid wave
  • Ix: paracentesis, ascitic fluid analysis (cell count and differential, albumin, total protein), serum ascites albumin gradient (SAAG)

metabolites in the blood and causing brain toxicity; often manifested with asterixis

hypoglycemia, portal/hepatic vein thrombosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, hypoxia, non-compliance

  • Common causes of ↑ bilirubin (HOT liver): hemolysis, obstruction, tumour, liver disease

Diseases

Conjugated

Dubin-Johnson syndrome: autosomal recessive condition caused by impaired intrahepatic bilirubin excretion

  • Absence of the canalicular protein multidrug-resistant protein 2 (MRP-2)

↑ serum direct

  • Functionally normal, enlarged, black (dark) liver; asymptomatic, chronic/recurrent jaundice
bilirubin (> 15%)
  • Dx: ↑ serum direct bilirubin, normal CBC, normal liver enzymes, grossly black liver on biopsy
Pathologic

Rotor syndrome: autosomal recessive condition caused by impaired hepatic storage of conjugated bilirubin, which leaks out

  • Phenotypically similar to Dubin-Johnson syndrome, but milder presentation; normal (regular) liver

Alagille syndrome: autosomal dominant condition caused by too few bile ducts to drain the bile, which leads to bile build-up in the liver

  • JAG1 or NOTCH2 gene mutations
  • Prominent forehead, triangular face, butterfly vertebrae, posterior embryotoxon, tetralogy of Fallot, pulmonary stenosis

Biliary tract obstruction: gallstones, cholangiocarcinoma, pancreatic cancer, liver cancer, liver fluke

Biliary tract disease: primary sclerosing cholangitis, primary biliary cholangitis

Unconjugated

Crigler-Najjar type 1: autosomal recessive condition caused by a complete lack of UDP-glucuronyl transferase, the enzyme responsible for

conjugation of indirect to direct bilirubin

↑ serum indirect

  • Normal appearing liver, severe jaundice at birth, colourless bile, kernicterus, lethargy, high-pitched cry
bilirubin
  • Dx: severe jaundice and icterus in a newborn with severely elevated serum indirect bilirubin
Physiologic or
  • Tx: phototherapy, exchange transfusions, heme oxygenase inhibitors, liver transplant prior to onset of brain damage
pathologic
  • Does NOT respond to phenobarbital
  • Fatal within 18 months after birth if untreated due to severe kernicterus

Crigler-Najjar type 2: less severe form of Crigler-Najjar type 1

  • Tx: phototherapy; responds to phenobarbital – ↑ liver enzyme synthesis (UDP-glucuronyl transferase)

Gilbert syndrome: autosomal recessive condition caused by transient reduction in hepatic UDP-glucuronyl transferase activity, which leads

to a decrease in bile conjugation/increase in indirect bilirubin

  • Asymptomatic, mild jaundice – usually an incidental finding in an otherwise healthy young male
  • Associated with stress, illness, strenuous exercise, and fasting
  • Dx: ↑ serum indirect bilirubin, normal CBC, normal liver enzymes

Hemolytic disease: sickle cell, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, spherocytosis, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia,

paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, ABO/Rh isoimmunization, autoimmune hemolytic anemia (warm and cold)

Ineffective erythropoiesis: vitamin B12/folate deficiency, porphyria, lead poisoning

Mixed

Acquired hepatocellular disease: cirrhosis, hepatitis, drugs (steroids, rifampin, probenecid, ribavirin), liver failure (sepsis)

  • Jaundice at birth is always pathologic– do NOT delay testing in any newborn with persistent jaundice beyond 2 weeks of age
  • Physiologic jaundice: occurs 48-72 hrs after birth, affects 50% of newborns, and is clinically benign; results from the relative

deficiency in UDP-glucuronyl transferase in the immature liver in newborns

Neoplastic liver masses
  • Most common tumours of the liver are metastatic – colorectal, pancreatic, lung, breast, melanoma
Benign

Hepatic adenoma: oral contraceptive use, anabolic steroid use, type I glycogen storage diseases/obesity

  • Surgery indicated if tumour is large, symptomatic, or high-risk features
  • HNF1-𝛼 inactivated adenomas = safest

Epithelial

  • Inflammatory adenomas = intermediate risk; upregulation of CRP and amyloid A
  • 𝜷-catenin activated adenoma = high risk

Bile duct adenoma

Non-epithelial

Hepatic hemangioma (most common): venous malformation; often an incidental finding, usually solitary

  • Dx: radiology; biopsy contraindicated due to risk of hemorrhage
  • Hepatocellular carcinoma (most common 1°): cirrhosis, viral hepatitis (HBV, HCV), tobacco smoking, alcohol,
Malignant

aflatoxin (Aspergillus flavus, Aspergillus parasiticus), males > 40 years

  • Asymptomatic, ↑ AFP (30-40%), thickened cell plates
  • Intrahepatic spread: direct invasion, vascular (portal and hepatic veins), bile ducts
  • Extrahepatic spread: hematogenous (lung, bone), lymphatic (porta hepatitis), direct, peritoneal
  • Tx: surgery, liver transplantation, radiofrequency ablation, transarterial chemoembolization, SBRT, sorafenib

Epithelial

Hepatoblastoma (most common in pediatrics): prematurity, low birth rate

  • ↑ AFP, enlarged abdomen, anorexia, weight loss
  • Tx: neoadjuvant therapy (chemotherapy, radiation), surgery, liver transplantation

Cholangiocarcinoma (intrahepatic bile ducts): PSC, ulcerative colitis, liver flukes, HCV, alcohol, HIV, gout, smoking

  • Presents late, poor Px

Angiosarcoma (blood vessels): thorotrast/vinyl chloride (PVC) exposure, arsenic, sex steroids; older males

Rhabdomyosarcoma (pediatrics)

Non-neoplastic liver masses
  • Focal nodular hyperplasia (benign): central stellate scar; females 35-50 years
  • Bile duct hamartoma (benign): von Meyenburg complex; multiple, small (< 0.5 cm), grey/white, irregular cystic lesions
  • Abscess: localized collection of pus (neutrophils, liquefied debris of dead cells, edema fluid)
